lesson.title: Reading the Trend: Correlation
lesson.summary: Correlation describes the strength and direction of the association between two variables shown in a scatterplot, but a correlation between two variables never by itself proves that one causes the other.
lesson.body:
Correlation is a description of how two variables tend to move together, based on the pattern of points in a scatterplot. Direction asks whether the y-values tend to increase as the x-values increase, called positive correlation, tend to decrease as the x-values increase, called negative correlation, or show no consistent pattern at all, called no correlation. Strength asks how closely the points cluster near a clear trend, a strong correlation, versus how loosely and widely they are scattered around that trend, a weak correlation.

Revisit the hours-studied scatterplot from the previous chapter. The five points climbed upward fairly tightly together, so that data set would be described as showing a strong positive correlation between hours studied and test score.

Here is the most important idea in this entire chapter: correlation is not causation. Two variables can be strongly correlated with each other without one of them causing the other. A classic illustration: during the summer months, both ice cream sales and reports of swimming related incidents tend to rise together, a clear positive correlation. But buying ice cream does not cause swimming incidents. Both variables are being pushed upward by a third factor entirely, hot weather, that happens to affect both of them at the same time. In general, an observed correlation between two variables might exist because one variable truly does affect the other, because both variables are being driven by some third factor, or simply because of coincidence within a limited data set, and a scatterplot alone can never tell you which of these explanations is the true one.

The most common and easiest correlation to spot, an upward trend where both variables rise together, gets its own closer look in the next chapter, positive correlation.
